book: 277 - Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink

chapters.relation: Miles argues that the popular 'porn is free speech applied to sex' defense (Wendy McElroy, Nadine Strossen) fails, using the contrast of Cohen's 'Fuck the Draft' jacket versus a hypothetical 'Schmoen' having public sex to express an opinion. He holds that political and religious speech persuade at a distance whereas public pornography coerces by making the unwilling audience actually perform the act of looking, so treating boobs like bumper stickers would be illiberal. The reasoning leans on a Millian harm/liberty framework: expression that merely offends is protected, but expression that forces others into an act crosses a line, so porn must be defended on privacy/autonomy grounds rather than as free speech.

Bartel asks whether a work can have artistic value BY VIRTUE OF its pornographic content, distinguishing a 'pornographic interest' (treating the medium as transparent, seeing through it to arousing content) from an 'artistic interest' (dwelling opaquely on the formal qualities of the medium, per Levinson). Using examples like Michelangelo's David, Elvgren pin-ups, and bondage photographs whose stillness doubles as a 'formal fetish', he concludes the two interests are incompatible: because a pornographic interest ignores form and an artistic interest attends to it, no work is good art in virtue of being good porn. He sets aside whether porn counts as 'art' (citing Rea) and the Sniffy-the-rat case on immoral art, treating value as a matter of the interest a beholder takes.

Howe distinguishes fine art, erotica, and pornography by the 'aesthetic distance' or disinterestedness the viewer can sustain, drawing on Schopenhauer's account of aesthetic contemplation (the perceiver dissolving individual will to become a 'pure subject' mirroring the object) and Bullough's 'psychical distance'. He argues pornography merely provokes vulgar genital arousal by exaggerating body parts out of gestalt balance (contra Feinberg, who allowed a painting to be both fine art and porn), so it forfeits disinterest entirely, while erotica provokes affection tied to romantic love and can approach fine art. Using Degas' Nude Study he concedes erotica and fine art differ only by degree, whereas pornography differs in kind because it permits no aesthetic attitude.

Rose takes a paradigm plotless YouPorn-style clip and tests the four standard charges against porn—obscenity, coercion/exploitation, harm to women, and harm to society—arguing each either collapses into cultural relativism or applies equally to any aesthetic object. He answers the feminist (MacKinnon/Dworkin-style) claim that porn subordinates women by noting that unjustified hierarchical power distorts the self-understanding of dominator and dominated alike (comparing it to 50 Cent's 'P.I.M.P.' and blaxploitation), so the wrong is not gender-specific. His conclusion is that porn should not be treated as different in kind from other art but judged aesthetically and morally by whether it distorts equitable social relationships, locating the real problem in capitalist cultural production rather than in porn as such.

Pipe traces how delivery technology reshaped pornography from 1970s adult theatres (Deep Throat, Behind the Green Door) that had to be 'vanilla' for a broad audience, through 1980s VHS and gonzo, 1990s DVD compilations, to Internet video-on-demand. His thesis is that each cheaper, more private medium let producers cater to ever-narrower niche fetishes ('Busty Latin Anal Nurses'), posing the driving question of whether technology serves pre-existing desire or manufactures new fetishes by showing audiences that such 'wonders' exist. The essay is a descriptive media history with little explicit philosophy, weighing gains (HD quality, privacy, choice) against losses (art, easy child access) and answering 'both' as to whether the changes are for better or worse.

Brophy warns of a coming 'pornographic singularity' when veridical, immersive, interactive, unbounded virtual reality (extrapolated from Second Life, Rapelay, and Sony's brain-stimulation patent) makes hypersex and hyper-romance supplant real intimacy. He uses Baudrillard's hyperreal/simulacra to explain how airbrushed models and 'pornbots' render real women 'just bad porn', invokes Nozick's experience machine as literally realized, and argues that utilitarianism and Kant's humanity formula fail to condemn using pornbots, so only Aristotelian virtue theory locates the wrong—the user malfunctions and cannot flourish as escalating deviance (furries, age-play, rape games) conditions vice. His bleak prophecy is that unbounded virtual desire will corrode families and community.

Parkhill challenges Jenefsky and Miller's second-wave feminist reading of Penthouse 'girl–girl' pictorials (that they present lesbians as sexually available to naturalize heterosexuality) by arguing that what some straight men enjoy is their own ABSENCE from the scene. He deploys Butler's 'Imitation and Gender Insubordination' to show mock-lesbian-wedding drag can subvert rather than confirm heterosexual 'originality', Foucault's repressive hypothesis and productive power to argue the lesbian is a product of, not outside, patriarchal norms, and Lacan-derived 'projective identification' and feminine jouissance to explain the male viewer's libidinal investment in his own ego-erasure. He concludes both the 'conqueror' and the self-shattering 'jouissance-chasing' pleasures coexist, and that girl–girl porn is ethically no different from ordinary hetero porn since the consumer still assumes a right of access to women's bodies.

Through the narrative of 'Aisha', a feminist who is aroused by SM imagery she has been taught to disown, Khan attacks the censorship of SM pornography and its 'monkey see, monkey do' harm hypothesis (citing declining rape rates). She names three state-inflicted harms: physical violence (prison sentences in Guglielmi and R. v. Brown), phenomenological violence—using Husserl and Merleau-Ponty's embodied phenomenology to argue courts dismiss submissives' lived reality as 'worthless'—and epistemic violence, using Foucault's power/knowledge to show how the Supreme Court of Canada in Little Sisters overrode expert and practitioner testimony about coded SM meaning. She argues SM consent and pleasure are real knowledge that censorship, aligned with MacKinnon/Dworkin anti-porn feminism, coercively erases.

In this interview, dominatrix-director Mz. Berlin answers the classic moral objections to porn from inside the industry: she rebuts objectification by insisting she chooses to be 'a commodity' and that choice makes it permissible, rejects the rape-myth/harm claim by citing declining rape rates and comparing porn to violent TV, and grounds BDSM's legitimacy entirely on INFORMED CONSENT, contrasting her voluntary waterboarding with her real torture abroad. Endorsing a strongly Millian self-ownership view ('my body is my own commodity'), she extends consent to selling kidneys, assisted suicide, and even display of her corpse, while drawing hard limits at sex with children, animals, or the dead where genuine informed consent is impossible. She also frames femdom porn as subverting male hegemony and normalizing fluid gender roles.

holes.name: Aesthetic Value and Aesthetic Attention
holes.what: The theory of what gives an object artistic/aesthetic value and the mode of attention (opaque, formal) proper to appreciating art, distinct from other interests.
holes.why: Chapter 27's entire argument turns on 'artistic interest' versus 'pornographic interest' and artistic value, a general aesthetics topic the taxonomy has no concept for (Kant's judgment-of-taste concept is narrower and unused here).

holes.name: Aesthetic Disinterestedness / Psychical Distance
holes.what: The doctrine that genuine aesthetic experience requires disinterested contemplation of an object for its own sake, at a psychical 'distance' from desire (Schopenhauer, Bullough).
holes.why: Chapter 28 makes disinterestedness/psychical distance the very criterion separating fine art and erotica from pornography, but the taxonomy has no concept for aesthetic disinterestedness.

holes.name: Jouissance
holes.what: The Lacanian/French-feminist notion of a radical, ego-shattering (coded feminine) pleasure distinct from ordinary comforting pleasure (plaisir).
holes.why: Chapter 34's core explanation of the male girl–girl porn consumer's pleasure is built on jouissance and its opposition to plaisir, a concept the taxonomy lacks despite listing Lacan.
